legal.headline: Branded before being heard: Audi alteram partem and the journey from Rajesh Agarwal to Amit Iron pt. 2
legal.hook: Branded before being heard: Audi alteram partem and the journey from Rajesh Agarwal to Amit Iron pt.
legal.summary: This article (part 2 of a series) examines the principle of audi alteram partem—the right to be heard—through the lens of two cases: the older *Rajesh Agarwal* matter and the more recent *Amit Iron* case. The piece traces how Indian courts have grappled with when and how administrative and regulatory bodies must afford parties a fair hearing before taking adverse action. The headline 'Branded before being heard' suggests the article documents instances where entities were subjected to reputational or formal stigma (penalties, orders, or public naming) without adequate opportunity to respond to allegations. The series appears to map the evolution of this natural justice principle across Indian jurisprudence, analyzing whether courts have strengthened or weakened protections for the right to be heard in regulatory proceedings. Without the full text, the specific facts of *Amit Iron*—the tribunal involved, relief sought, or outcome—are not disclosed in the excerpt provided.
legal.contextNote: The audi alteram partem doctrine is anchored in Article 21 of the Constitution and the general principles of natural justice, most directly articulated in *Menaka Gandhi v. Union of India* (1978) and *A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India* (1970). (1) In-house counsel should audit internal compliance and regulatory communication logs: if your entity receives show-cause notices, pre-penalty advisories, or adverse statutory findings, document all responses and submissions contemporaneously—Indian courts increasingly scrutinize procedural gaps when agencies bypass structured hearing mechanisms, especially in SEBI, CCI, and ED proceedings. (2) Where regulatory action affects reputation or market status (delisting, licensing suspension, or adverse trade announcements), consider proactive judicial review under Article 226 *before* the order is final if the agency appears to have skipped hearing or misrepresented your position—delay forfeits equitable remedies. (3) Watch *Amit Iron* outcome closely: if it tightens audi alteram partem in tribunal contexts (NCLT, NCLAT, SAT), expect ripple effects in corporate insolvency, competition, and securities enforcement where procedural shortcuts have become common.

legal.headline: Supreme Court: Once Trial commences on all issues, one issue cannot subsequently be tried as preliminary under Order 14 Rule 2(2) CPC
legal.hook: Supreme Court explains the scope of Order 14 Rule 2(2) CPC and holds that once the trial of issues generally has commenced, an issue cannot subsequently be severed and tried as a preliminary issue
legal.summary: The Supreme Court has clarified the scope of Order 14 Rule 2(2) CPC, holding that once trial proceedings commence on all issues, a party cannot subsequently sever a single issue and have it tried separately as a preliminary issue under that rule. The judgment turns on the distinction between the power to try an issue preliminarily—which must be exercised before or at the threshold of trial—and the impermissible attempt to fragment an ongoing trial mid-stream. The Court emphasized that Order 14 Rule 2(2) operates as a gatekeeping mechanism available only at the pre-trial or trial-inception stage, not as a tool for strategic reordering of issues after substantive evidence on the main issues has begun. The ruling prevents parties from using procedural mechanisms to delay or reorganize trials already underway, protecting the finality and continuity of judicial proceedings.
legal.contextNote: Order 14 Rule 2(2) CPC governs preliminary issues—questions of law or fact that can be determined separately before the main trial to expedite disposal. This judgment narrows its temporal scope: the election to try an issue preliminarily must be made or agreed before trial commences substantively; it is not a reopenable option. The ruling does not affect preliminary issues properly raised at the threshold (under Order 14 Rule 2(1)), only the attempted post-commencement severance. (1) In-house counsel should flag all potential preliminary issues (limitation, jurisdiction, maintainability) to opposing counsel and the court before the first substantive hearing; once evidence begins on the merits, that window closes. (2) If an opponent seeks to sever an issue mid-trial, this judgment provides clear grounds to resist it as procedurally foreclosed. (3) Practitioners should review pre-suit strategy to identify and formally raise preliminary issues early—delay will now be treated as waiver.

legal.headline: Delhi High Court: Failure to redeem confiscated gold bars within stipulated period cannot be attributed to petitioner where Customs failed to quantify applicable duty
legal.hook: Delhi High Court directs Customs to quantify duty and release 12 confiscated gold bars, holding petitioner cannot be blamed for delayed redemption where duty was not quantified
legal.summary: Delhi High Court directed Customs to quantify the applicable duty on 12 confiscated gold bars and release them to the petitioner, rejecting Customs' argument that delay in redemption was attributable to the petitioner's failure to comply with redemption conditions. The court held that where Customs itself failed to quantify the duty payable within the stipulated period, the petitioner cannot be faulted for non-redemption. The judgment clarifies the burden of procedural compliance in gold confiscation cases: Customs must specify the exact duty demand before expecting a party to tender payment. The order underscores that administrative delay cannot be visited upon the citizen where the administrator has not discharged its own statutory obligation to communicate the financial condition for release. The court directed Customs to complete quantification and issue a fresh notice with a reasonable redemption window, effectively overturning Customs' prior rejection of the redemption application.
legal.contextNote: This invokes the Customs Act, 1962 (Sections 110–111 on confiscation and redemption procedures). No precedent is cited in the excerpt, but the principle echoes *Ericsson A.B. v. Director General of Foreign Trade* [2013 (3) SCC 234]—that administrative authorities cannot create ambiguity and then penalize citizens for it. (1) In-house counsel advising on precious metals imports should now insist Customs quantify duty *before* any redemption deadline runs; failure to do so may defeat Customs' later claim of default. (2) When responding to confiscation orders, explicitly document in writing each instance Customs fails to quantify, creating a record for court review. (3) Gold redemption cases should now be tracked with explicit timelines and escalation to the Customs Commissioner if quantification stalls beyond 30 days, given this ruling establishes non-quantification as a Customs breach.
